 What Is ReactOS? How It Works and How to Try It Safely
 By Marcus Pruitt 
 Published November 3, 2026 
 Preferred source 
 Share 
 Share 
 Windows 10 reached end of support in October 2025, and many people still rely on older Windows software and hardware. If you've searched "what is ReactOS," you're likely wondering whether this free alternative can run those programs.
 ReactOS is an open source operating system built to run Windows apps and drivers without Microsoft's proprietary code. It's still in alpha, but version 0.4.16 makes it easier to try than any release before it. Below, I explain how it works, what runs well, how to test it safely, and who it suits.
 What Is ReactOS?
 The ReactOS operating system is written from scratch to be binary compatible with the Windows NT family. In practice, that means a Windows program (an .exe file) or a Windows driver should install and run on ReactOS the same way it would on Windows, with no emulator sitting in between.
 ReactOS isn't built on Linux, even though sites like DistroWatch list it alongside Linux distributions. Many Windows-like OS projects are Linux distributions with a Windows-style theme on top. ReactOS uses its own NT-style kernel and boots straight into a desktop that looks and behaves like Windows 2000 or Windows XP. The codebase is licensed mainly under GPL 2.0 and developed in the open on GitHub , and official release images are free to download.
 How ReactOS Works (and Where Wine Fits In)
 The core of ReactOS is its own hybrid kernel, built to match the Windows NT architecture. The Win32 graphics subsystem, the boot loader, and the ReactOS Explorer shell are also the project's own code.
 For many user-mode libraries, ReactOS borrows code from Wine , the compatibility layer Linux and macOS users rely on to run Windows apps. On Linux, Wine translates Windows API calls into calls a Unix-like system understands. ReactOS uses its own fork of Wine that talks directly to a Windows-like kernel, so there is nothing to translate. That design is also why ReactOS can load real Windows drivers, something Wine on Linux cannot do.
 The compatibility target has been Windows Server 2003 (NT 5.2) for most of the project's life. Toward the end of the 0.4.15 cycle, the team relaxed that rule so it could update its Wine fork from the 2.x and 3.x era toward Wine 10.0, and 0.4.16 includes a large share of that work. Official release images are still built with Windows Server 2003 exports only, and support for Vista-era and newer apps remains an experimental build option for developers.
 ReactOS vs Windows vs Linux With Wine
 Here is how ReactOS compares with Windows 11 and with running Windows apps on Linux through Wine.
 ReactOS Windows 11 Linux with Wine 
 Price Free Paid license (often preinstalled) Free 
 Kernel Own NT-compatible kernel Windows NT Linux 
 Runs Windows apps Many XP-era apps, hit or miss Yes, except 16-bit apps Many, via a translation layer 
 Runs Windows drivers Some XP/2003-era drivers Modern signed 64-bit drivers only No 
 Stability Alpha, not for daily use Stable Stable 
 Best for Testing, legacy software, learning NT Everyday use Everyday use without Windows 
 A Short History of ReactOS
 ReactOS started life around 1996 as FreeWin95, a project to clone Windows 95 that stalled in design debates without releasing a single build. In 1998, its members relaunched it under a new name with a new goal: reimplementing Windows NT. The "React" in the name refers to the group's reaction against Microsoft's dominant position in the market.
 Year Milestone 
 1996 FreeWin95 project begins 
 1998 Relaunched as ReactOS, targeting Windows NT 
 2006 Version 0.3.0, first release with official networking support 
 2016 Version 0.4.0 adds a new Explorer shell and theming 
 2021 Version 0.4.14 (December 16) 
 2025 Version 0.4.15 (March 21) 
 2026 Version 0.4.16 (August 29) with a graphical installer 
 The gaps between releases are long. It took more than three years to get from 0.4.14 to the 0.4.15 update in March 2025 , and another 18 months to reach 0.4.16. ReactOS runs on volunteer work and donations, with the ReactOS Deutschland e.V. association occasionally funding contracts for specific tasks, such as full-time work on the new graphical installer.
 What's New in ReactOS 0.4.16
 Version 0.4.16 is the most approachable ReactOS release to date and the biggest ReactOS development update of 2026. According to the official 0.4.16 release announcement , the headline changes are:
 Graphical installer and an all-in-one image: the separate LiveCD and BootCD downloads are merged, so you can test and install ReactOS from the same image.
 Better graphics driver support: a long-running slowdown with Nvidia drivers is fixed, as is a bug that left OpenGL windows blank on AMD drivers.
 HD audio: a new HD audio bus driver means controllers that work with Windows XP and Server 2003 drivers should now work in ReactOS.
 New storage driver: a new ATA driver lets ReactOS boot in far more environments, including Hyper-V Generation 1 virtual machines, and a Disk Cleanup utility joins the system tools.
 Networking: asynchronous connection support improves both network performance and app compatibility.
 Server Core install type: a new option that skips the graphical Explorer shell, similar to Windows Server Core.
 16-bit app support: release images now include WineVDM, which improves compatibility with 16-bit Windows programs.
 The release resolves 381 bug reports and includes 2,808 commits.
 What ReactOS Is Like to Use
 If you used a PC in the early 2000s, ReactOS will feel familiar. You get a classic Start menu and taskbar, a Windows-style file manager, Control Panel, Device Manager, and built-in apps such as Notepad, Paint, Calculator, Command Prompt, Spider Solitaire, and a Minesweeper clone called WineMine.
 Stability is where the alpha label shows. Expect crashes, blue-screen bugchecks, programs that refuse to install, and hardware that has no working driver. The project's own download page warns that ReactOS provides no guarantee of stability, of safety for your files, or that it will work on your hardware at all.
 Installing Apps With the Applications Manager
 ReactOS ships with the Applications Manager (RAPPS), a built-in catalog that downloads and installs tested versions of popular free programs. I recommend starting there. Installers downloaded straight from the web are hit or miss, while the catalog versions are often older but more likely to work.
 Plenty of Windows software does run. Older releases of Adobe Reader, GIMP, and LibreOffice are among the programs known to work. The project's advice is to test the specific app you care about in a virtual machine before relying on it.
 How to Try ReactOS Safely
 The safest way to try ReactOS is in a virtual machine, and the project itself recommends this if the computer holds anything you can't afford to lose.
 System Requirements
 The official ReactOS system requirements are extremely light by modern standards. The installation guide lists these minimums:
 Processor: x86 (Pentium or later) or x64, though development focuses on 32-bit x86 first and ReactOS 64-bit support comes from a separate AMD64 port
 RAM: 64 MB minimum, 256 MB recommended, and 2 GB if you want to test large software suites
 Storage: 450 MB of free space on an IDE or SATA drive, with a FAT16 or FAT32 boot partition
 Graphics: a VGA-compatible card (VESA BIOS 2.0 or later)
 Option 1: Run It in a Virtual Machine (Recommended)
 Download the 0.4.16 release image from the ReactOS download page . If the download arrives as a ZIP archive, extract the ISO first.
 Create a new virtual machine. A ReactOS VirtualBox setup is a good free option, and VMware, QEMU, and Hyper-V (Generation 1) also work. Give it at least 256 MB of RAM and a few gigabytes of disk space.
 Boot the VM from the ISO, then choose the Live environment to explore ReactOS without installing, or start the setup to install it to the virtual disk.
 Some antivirus programs flag ReactOS files as malicious. The project documents these as false positives.
 Option 2: Install It on Spare Hardware
 Only install ReactOS on a machine with no data you need. The ReactOS installation guide lists several limitations worth checking first:
 UEFI firmware isn't supported yet, so the PC must boot in legacy BIOS mode.
 Setup expects a FAT16 or FAT32 boot partition by default. Booting from Btrfs has been possible since 0.4.10 but remains experimental.
 Some SATA controllers are not detected, and the boot partition works best as the first partition on a single disk.
 The setup program won't stop you from performing destructive disk operations.
 To create installation media, write the ISO to a USB drive with a tool such as Rufus, and check the project's supported hardware list before you start. Developers who want the newest fixes can use nightly builds, which are built from every commit but are more likely to contain regressions, or they can compile ReactOS from source.
 Is ReactOS Legal and Safe?
 ReactOS is designed to stay within copyright law by using clean-room reverse engineering. The team works out how Windows behaves and writes its own code to match, without copying Microsoft's. Anyone who has seen leaked Microsoft source code, including the Windows NT 3.5, NT 4, and Windows 2000 leaks or the Windows Research Kernel, is barred from contributing.
 In 2006, after a developer alleged that some code had been derived from disassembled Windows binaries, the project temporarily locked its code repository, audited its codebase, and required every developer to sign an agreement to follow its reverse-engineering policy.
 Safety is a different matter. As alpha software, ReactOS can corrupt data, and it doesn't receive the kind of security patching that a mainstream operating system gets. I wouldn't use it for banking, email, or any files that matter. On privacy, the project says ReactOS doesn't track user data, and its source code is open for anyone to check.
 Who Is ReactOS For?
 With Windows 10 support having ended on October 14, 2025 , plenty of people are asking whether ReactOS is a free way to keep running Windows software on an older PC. For an everyday computer, our answer is no, at least not yet. Windows 11 on supported hardware, a Linux distribution with Wine , and Microsoft's Extended Security Updates program for Windows 10 (which now runs until October 12, 2027) are all safer choices today.
 ReactOS makes sense for:
 Retro computing and preservation fans who want to run Windows XP and Server 2003-era software and drivers on hardware that modern Windows won't support.
 Developers and students who want to see how Windows NT internals work through an open source reimplementation.
 Contributors who want to help build it. The project welcomes coders, testers, and translators.
 Curious Windows users with a spare virtual machine and an afternoon to explore.
 The preservation angle is the strongest case for the project. As Microsoft drops support for older software and drivers, an open source Windows alternative with NT compatibility keeps that software runnable long after the original platform is gone.
 ReactOS Questions & Answers
 Still have questions? Here are short answers to the most common ones about ReactOS, from whether it's Linux and which apps it runs to dual-booting, legality, and where to download it.
 Is ReactOS Linux?
 No. ReactOS is written from scratch and is not built on Linux or any Unix system. It uses its own Windows NT-compatible kernel.
 Can ReactOS Run Windows 10 or Windows 11 Apps?
 Mostly no. Official release images target Windows Server 2003-level compatibility, so software from the Windows XP era runs best. Support for apps that need Vista and newer APIs is still experimental.
 Can I Dual-Boot ReactOS With Windows?
 It is technically possible, but it needs legacy BIOS mode and, by default, a FAT16 or FAT32 boot partition, and the installer doesn't prevent destructive disk changes. I recommend a virtual machine or a spare PC instead.
 Is ReactOS Legal?
 Yes, downloading and using ReactOS is legal. The project relies on clean-room reverse engineering and bars anyone who has seen leaked Microsoft source code from contributing.
 Why Is ReactOS Still in Alpha After So Many Years?
 Reimplementing Windows NT with binary compatibility is an enormous job for a volunteer team, and the project prioritizes getting compatibility right over shipping quickly. Its documentation still warns of possible data loss.
 Where Can I Download ReactOS?
 Release images and nightly builds are available from the official ReactOS website. The project does not sell or distribute official installation media, so you create your own from the ISO.
 Should You Try ReactOS? Our Verdict
 ReactOS 0.4.16 is worth downloading if you are curious about Windows internals, want to run old Windows software and drivers, or simply want to see how far a 30-year volunteer effort has come. The new graphical installer and the combined live image make this the easiest ReactOS release to try so far. Run it in a virtual machine, keep your expectations at alpha level, and use a supported operating system for your everyday computing.
